title: The tower
hook: a man retires to a round tower with his books to write about himself

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tao Te Ching closed. Your line was like water. Today, a new book and a new voice.

A round stone tower at the corner of a French country house. A chapel on the ground floor, a bedroom above it, and on the top floor a round library: shelves curving around the walls, a desk, windows over the yard and the fields. A nobleman named Michel de Montaigne climbs the stairs, shuts the door, and starts to write. His subject isn't war, or God, or the public duties he has just walked away from. His subject is himself: his habits, his moods, his kidney stones, his cat. And he gives what he makes up there a modest name.
screen: `A ROUND STONE TOWER.` → `A LIBRARY AT THE TOP.` → `HIS SUBJECT IS HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the date on the wall. Montaigne had a Latin inscription put up in his study, and it gives the details itself: in the year 1571, at the age of thirty-eight, on his birthday, weary of the court and of public duties, he withdrew to the company of the learned Muses, to spend what was left of his life in calm and freedom. He wrote his retirement onto the wall, so he'd see it. Second, the word. He called the pieces he wrote essais. In his French, an essai is a try, a test, an attempt. He wasn't handing down finished answers. He was trying his judgment out on a subject, the way you'd test the ice with one foot. Third, the back room. In his essay on solitude, Montaigne says we should keep a room behind the shop, all our own, entirely free, where we can talk with ourselves. Keep a wife, children, goods, he says, and health if you can, but don't tie yourself so tightly that your happiness depends on them. The tower was his back room made of stone. Fourth, the tower without the stone. Hardly anyone has one. But a car in a parking lot for ten minutes, a bench, the first quiet half hour before the house wakes: those are towers too. Montaigne didn't leave people; he went on living with his family. His point is that there's a room in you that doesn't belong to anyone's to-do list.
screen: `1571, ON THE WALL.` · `ESSAI MEANS A TRY.` · `A ROOM BEHIND THE SHOP.` · `A TOWER CAN BE A PARKED CAR.` · then, large: `MY TOWER.`

segments.voice: Make wherever you are a little more yours: turn your phone face down, close a door if there is one, or turn your chair toward a wall or a window. Then ask Montaigne's kind of question about yourself, with no need for an answer: what am I like this morning, tired, curious, sore, glad? It's only a try, an essai.
Essai. Montaigne's French word for what he wrote in his tower: a try, a test, an attempt at a subject. Today's word.
Your line: my tower. A tower doesn't need stone walls, only a door that's yours. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne take his tower and his 'room behind the shop' as a model for keeping a private space, inner or outer, where a person can think about their own life in freedom.

chat.says: Why did Montaigne call his writing essais? Isn't that just a school assignment?
options: In his French, essai meant a try: he was testing his judgment, not giving answers.
He meant they were final answers, so readers would never need to ask again.
He was a teacher, and essais were the exercises he set for students at court.

notes: First day of Block B (Montaigne). The index hook includes 'in 1571, aged 38'; the script states those only as what Montaigne's own study inscription says. Confirm the inscription's wording (the last day of February, his birthday, aged 38, 1571).

The tower's layout (chapel, bedroom, round library on top, with a view) is drawn from Essays 3.3; confirm. Kidney stones and his cat are subjects in the Essays (2.37; 2.12); confirm before keeping the list.

'Essai' glossed as a try, test, attempt; this is the ordinary French sense and is how Montaigne uses it, but it is a word-meaning claim. The word segment links essai to English 'essay'; a standard-lexicon etymology, flagged under the claims rule for a scholar to confirm or cut.
Essays numbering follows the path's outline; editions number some chapters differently.
Montaigne is paraphrased throughout; Cotton/Hazlitt and Florio are public domain but not on the validator's translation list.
